did_you_know.text: The eighth day came after seven days of preparation for Aaron and his sons, when they stayed at the entrance of the Tent of Meeting. It marked the beginning of their public service as priests.
The Sages and Rashi saw the calf offered here as a reminder of repairing the sin of the Golden Calf. The priests’ service thus also became a symbol of atonement for a past crisis.
In Biblical Hebrew, the word minḥah can mean a gift or tribute, and in Leviticus it also refers to a grain offering. Here, it is mixed with oil.
The “horns of the altar” were not animal horns but projections at the altar’s corners. Blood was placed on them as part of the sin-offering ritual.
Even during the dedication ceremony of the Tabernacle, the regular morning offering continued. This shows that the special event was integrated into the daily order of worship.
The word tenufah describes a ritual presentation of parts of the offering before God, not merely waving them in the air. The breast and right thigh were given a special role in the ceremony.
The Sages connected Aaron’s blessing here with the priestly blessing stated explicitly in the Book of Numbers. Raising the hands later became a familiar sign of a priestly blessing.
In later interpretation, the fire from the holy place was seen as a sign that the offerings had been accepted. The people’s response combines great joy with awe.
